setting: A civil trial concerns a damaged rented piano. A neighbor repeats a nonparty delivery driver’s casual remark to prove who dropped it; the driver was not employed by either party.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the driver tell you that afternoon?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: He said, "Mara dropped the piano off the lift."

explanation: The driver's out-of-court assertion is offered to prove Mara dropped the piano.
trap_note: Personally hearing the remark does not establish that its accusation is true.

setting: A civil trial concerns missing wedding photographs. The photographer's friend repeats an absent guest's description to prove the camera was stolen.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the guest say happened to the camera?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: She told me a man in a green coat took it.

explanation: The guest's account is an out-of-court assertion offered for its truth.
trap_note: The friend may know what was said without knowing who took the camera.

setting: A criminal theft trial concerns a missing bronze bell. An officer repeats a calm anonymous tip to prove the defendant sold it; no other use is offered.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the caller tell you?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "Oren sold that bell at the river market."

explanation: The anonymous accusation cannot prove the sale merely by being repeated by an officer.
trap_note: The officer's official position does not create a hearsay exception.

setting: A civil trial concerns a collapsed deck. A visitor recounts a nonparty carpenter’s later guess to establish that bolts were missing; the carpenter had no role in building the deck.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the carpenter say caused the collapse?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: He said, "They must have left out half the bolts."

explanation: The carpenter's later assertion is offered as proof of the missing bolts.
trap_note: A witness cannot turn another person's assertion into admissible testimony by quoting it.

setting: A civil trial concerns a scratched display case. A shopper repeats a friend's account the next week to prove that an employee used a metal scraper.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did your friend tell you about the scratch?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: She said the clerk dragged a scraper right across the glass.

explanation: The friend's later account is being offered for the truth of what it describes.
trap_note: Relevance to the scratch does not resolve hearsay.

setting: A civil trial concerns a leaking roof. An authenticated customer comment is offered to prove that the installer skipped the flashing, and no exception is established.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What does this comment say?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "The crew never put flashing around the chimney."

explanation: Authenticating a comment does not make its factual assertion admissible for its truth.
trap_note: Knowing who wrote a statement solves a different problem from hearsay.

setting: A criminal trial concerns a forged parking permit. An investigator repeats a colleague's account of what a guard said to prove the defendant printed it.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did your colleague report?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: She said the guard told her, "I watched Niko print that permit."

explanation: Both layers of this account need an applicable hearsay exception, and neither has one here.
trap_note: A second retelling does not erase the first layer of hearsay.

setting: A civil trial concerns a spoiled shipment. A business log records an outside tourist's unverified statement about the truck's refrigeration.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What does the log report?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "Visitor says the driver switched the cooler off before leaving."

explanation: The business record exception does not automatically cover the outside visitor's embedded statement.
trap_note: A regularly kept document can still contain a separate hearsay layer.

setting: A civil trial concerns a stolen painting. A witness repeats a voicemail from an absent friend to prove the gallery owner hid it.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the voicemail say?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "I saw the owner put the painting in her car yesterday."

explanation: The friend's recorded assertion is offered to prove the owner's conduct.
trap_note: Recording a statement does not itself make it admissible.

setting: A civil trial concerns a tenant's broken window. A neighbor repeats a child's statement made calmly two days later to prove who threw the stone.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the child tell you on Monday?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: He said, "My cousin threw the stone on Saturday."

explanation: The child's later account is an out-of-court assertion offered for its truth.
trap_note: Youth alone supplies no hearsay exception.

setting: A civil trial concerns disputed overtime. A worker repeats another employee's personal estimate, made outside any job responsibility, to establish the hours worked.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did your coworker say about your hours?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: She told me, "You probably worked fifty hours that week."

explanation: The coworker's outside estimate is offered as proof of the hours without an applicable exception.
trap_note: Not every statement by an employee concerns a matter within the scope of employment.

setting: A civil trial concerns damage to a kayak. A witness repeats a repair customer's casual opinion to prove the owner caused the crack.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the customer say while you waited?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "The owner must have dragged it over rocks."

explanation: The customer's out-of-court explanation is offered to establish how the crack happened.
trap_note: An opinion can be a hearsay assertion just as a factual description can.

setting: A civil trial concerns a dented elevator door. A witness quotes an absent resident's signed letter to identify the mover responsible.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the resident write?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "I watched the mover ram the trolley into the door."

explanation: The signed letter contains an out-of-court assertion offered for its truth.
trap_note: A signature establishes authorship rather than a hearsay exception.

setting: A criminal trial concerns stolen laboratory equipment. A witness repeats what an absent student claimed in a private message to prove the theft.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the message say?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "I saw Devin leave with the microscope under his jacket."

explanation: The message is an out-of-court assertion offered to prove Devin took the microscope.
trap_note: A private message is still a statement under the hearsay rules.

setting: A civil trial concerns a damaged greenhouse. A witness repeats a nonparty contractor’s account of what an assistant said, offered to prove the tenant unplugged the heater; neither speaker worked for a party.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the contractor tell you?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "My assistant says the tenant pulled the heater's plug."

explanation: Each speaker's assertion needs its own basis for admission, and none is established.
trap_note: The contractor's experience does not cure a secondhand factual account.

setting: A civil trial concerns a missing cash deposit. A manager offers a routine incident report containing an unknown caller's accusation, solely to prove the accusation.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Read the caller's statement in your report.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "The cashier kept the deposit in her coat pocket."

explanation: A routine report does not automatically admit an unknown caller's accusation for its truth.
trap_note: The report's business purpose does not establish the caller's reliability.

setting: A civil trial concerns a damaged sculpture. An owner's friend recounts the owner's self-serving statement, offered by that same owner to deny responsibility.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the owner tell you afterward?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "I never touched the sculpture; it fell by itself."

explanation: A party cannot use the opposing-party rule to introduce that party's own statement in support of the party's case.
trap_note: The opposing-party exclusion applies when the statement is offered against its speaker's side.

setting: A civil trial concerns a signed delivery receipt. The receipt's note about an absent bystander's observation is offered to prove the parcel was opened.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What does the handwritten note say?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "A bystander told me the courier opened the parcel on the street."

explanation: The bystander's assertion remains a separate hearsay layer even if the receipt itself qualifies as a record.
trap_note: One admissible layer does not automatically admit every statement inside it.

setting: A criminal trial concerns a warehouse alarm. A witness recounts an absent acquaintance's later story to prove the defendant disabled it.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did your acquaintance say last month?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "Tavi told me he saw the defendant cut the alarm wire."

explanation: This retelling contains two unsupported hearsay layers.
trap_note: Repeating a named source is not the same as presenting that source's testimony.

setting: A civil trial concerns a disputed fence line. A party offers a recent email from an absent surveyor as proof of the boundary, without qualifying it as a record or expert testimony.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the surveyor write to you?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "The fence sits two feet inside your parcel."

explanation: The email's boundary assertion is offered for its truth without a demonstrated exception.
trap_note: Professional expertise alone does not exempt an out-of-court statement from hearsay rules.

setting: A civil trial concerns spoiled flowers. A florist repeats a customer's casual remark to establish the van's temperature.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the customer tell you?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "That van was warmer than my kitchen when they opened it."

explanation: The customer's assertion about temperature is offered for its truth.
trap_note: Sensory descriptions can still be hearsay when repeated by someone else.

setting: A civil trial concerns a missing tool chest. A witness quotes an absent mechanic's note to establish that a particular truck carried it away.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the note say?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "I saw your chest in the back of the orange truck."

explanation: The mechanic's written observation is an out-of-court statement offered for its truth.
trap_note: The note's specificity does not supply an exception.

setting: A civil trial concerns an injury on a staircase. A witness repeats a building visitor's calm account a week later to prove a step was loose.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the visitor tell you afterward?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "The third step moved when I stood on it."

explanation: The visitor's later description is offered to prove the condition of the step.
trap_note: A statement about a relevant condition is not automatically admissible.

setting: A civil trial concerns a late parcel. A witness quotes an absent neighbor's social-media post to establish the delivery time.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What time did the post say the courier arrived?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: It said, "The courier finally came at ten last night."

explanation: The post's factual assertion is offered for its truth.
trap_note: Public availability does not create a hearsay exception.

setting: A civil trial concerns a contaminated tank. A supervisor repeats a rumor passed through two unnamed workers to prove who poured solvent into it.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: How did you hear who filled the tank?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: One worker said another worker had seen Jules pour solvent in.

explanation: Each out-of-court assertion needs an admissible basis, which this chain of rumor lacks.
trap_note: The number of people repeating an accusation does not make it firsthand evidence.

setting: A civil trial concerns a bicycle collision. The plaintiff offers the defendant cyclist's own words against the cyclist.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the cyclist say when you spoke?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "I was looking at my phone when I hit you."

explanation: The cyclist's own statement may be offered against that cyclist as an opposing-party statement.
trap_note: The speaker need not have intended to make a legal admission.

setting: A civil trial concerns a fire at a pottery studio. A visitor describes what an injured worker cried out while flames were still spreading.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the worker shout as you helped her out?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "The kiln just burst into flames!"

explanation: The statement describes the startling fire while the worker was still under its stress.
trap_note: An excited utterance can be admitted even when the speaker is available to testify.

setting: A civil trial concerns a flooded cellar. A witness repeats a warning only to explain why she moved the stored paintings, not to prove water was present.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: Why did you move the paintings upstairs?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: A neighbor called, "There's water coming under your door!"

explanation: The warning is offered for its effect on the listener rather than to prove the warning true.
trap_note: A quoted statement is not hearsay when its truth is not the point of offering it.

setting: A civil trial concerns a restaurant burn. A treating nurse recounts the patient's description of symptoms given to obtain treatment.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the patient tell you during the examination?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "My hand burns, and I can't bend these two fingers."

explanation: The symptom description was made for medical treatment and was pertinent to that treatment.
trap_note: The medical-treatment exception covers pertinent symptoms as well as some accounts of their cause.

setting: A civil trial concerns a boat departure. A dock worker describes the passenger's statement of a current travel plan, offered to show the passenger's intent at that moment.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did the passenger say before leaving the desk?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "I'm taking the noon ferry to the island."

explanation: The statement expresses a then-existing plan rather than a memory of a past event.
trap_note: The exception distinguishes current intent from a backward-looking factual claim.

setting: A civil trial concerns a collision outside a café. A witness repeats what her companion said while watching the vehicles approach.

transcript.speaker: Q
transcript.text: What did your companion say as you both watched?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: "That blue car is coming into our lane right now."

explanation: The statement describes an event while the speaker was perceiving it.
trap_note: A present-sense impression need not involve an excited or frightened speaker.
